nameStory: Dogfennel gets its curious name from its feathery, thread-like leaves that somewhat resemble fennel, though it's not related to that herb at all. The "dog" prefix was historically added to plants that were considered inferior or wild versions of more useful species. Despite the dismissive name, this native plant plays an important role in natural ecosystems.
description: Dogfennel is a tall, wispy perennial that looks almost like a green feather duster growing in your garden. It typically stands 2-6 feet tall with multiple branching stems rising from a sturdy base. The most striking feature is its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves that create delicate, lacy patterns along the stems. Small clusters of tiny white flowers appear at the top of the plant in late summer and fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are so finely divided they look like green threads or pine needles arranged in intricate, fractal-like patterns along the stem. When you crush them between your fingers, they release a distinctive sour smell reminiscent of dill pickles.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multiple upright stems branch from a substantial woody base, creating a bushy, fountain-like appearance that can reach 6 feet tall in good conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flower heads clustered at branch tips have a subtle, pleasant floral fragrance - much sweeter than the sour-smelling leaves.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, branching stems are densely covered with the thread-like foliage, giving the whole plant a soft, feathery texture when brushed against.

habitat: In New England, dogfennel is quite rare and typically found in disturbed soils, field edges, and waste areas, particularly in warmer, protected locations. It prefers sandy or well-drained soils and full sun exposure. This southern species is at the northern edge of its range here, so it's most likely to appear in the warmer microclimates of southern New England.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as delicate, thread-like shoots from the woody base, creating an increasingly feathery appearance as stems elongate.
seasonality.summer: Plant reaches full height with lush, finely-divided foliage. The distinctive pickle-like scent is strongest during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Small white flowers bloom in clusters at branch tips from late summer through fall, followed by tiny seeds with fluffy white bristles.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, leaving dried stems and the persistent woody base that will sprout again in spring.

funFact: Despite being called "fennel," this plant smells exactly like dill pickles when you crush its leaves - a scent so distinctive that once you smell it, you'll never forget this plant or mistake it for anything else!
confusionNotes: The thread-like leaves might remind you of asparagus foliage or wild carrot leaves, but dogfennel's distinctive pickle smell when crushed is a dead giveaway. Remember: if it smells like pickles, it's dogfennel!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - dogfennel has absolutely nothing to do with cooking fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) and doesn't belong in your spice rack. This is purely a wild ornamental plant that happens to share a common name due to its feathery appearance.
compareHints: Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves. Common boneset has large, wrinkled leaves that actually wrap around the stem, while dogfennel looks more like a delicate fern or asparagus plant. The pickle-scented foliage also sets it apart from any of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base.

Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.

Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets.
Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves.
Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
